ai.definition: Whole Brain Emulation (WBE) is the theoretical process of creating a functional copy or simulation of a human brain, including all its synaptic connections and neural activity patterns, within a computer system. The goal is to replicate the cognitive functions of a physical brain in a digital environment.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves high-resolution mapping of the brain's connectome (the network of connections between neurons) at the synaptic level followed by the simulation of this structure on neuromorphic computing substrates, which are designed to mimic the biological neural networks more closely than traditional computers.
ai.problemSolved: WBE addresses the challenge of preserving or transferring human consciousness and memories for potential digital immortality or backup purposes. It also has implications for understanding brain function, treating neurological disorders, and developing advanced artificial intelligence systems.
ai.manufacturing: Currently, WBE is in the theoretical stage with no practical manufacturing processes available. The technology requires advancements in neuroimaging techniques, data storage capabilities, and neuromorphic computing hardware.
ai.buildProcess: The build process would involve creating a detailed map of the brain's structure and function using advanced imaging technologies like MRI or even more specialized methods such as serial two-photon tomography (STP). This data would then be translated into a digital model that can be run on neuromorphic hardware.
ai.costDrivers: The primary cost drivers are expected to include high-resolution neuroimaging, data storage for the vast amount of synaptic information, and the development of advanced neuromorphic computing technologies. These costs could range from millions to billions depending on the scale and complexity of the project.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in a very early stage of research and development with significant scientific and technological hurdles to overcome before practical applications can be realized.
ai.regulation: There are no current regulatory frameworks for WBE, as the technology does not yet exist at a level that requires regulation. However, if developed, it could raise ethical, legal, and societal issues that would need addressing through new regulations.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges in accurately mapping and simulating the brain's complexity, potential loss of personal identity or consciousness during the emulation process, and ethical concerns related to the creation of digital copies of human beings.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently speculative due to the lack of practical applications. If WBE were to become viable, it could potentially open up new markets in healthcare, technology, and even insurance, but this would depend on overcoming numerous technical and ethical barriers.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving neuroimaging technologies, developing more efficient neuromorphic computing architectures, and addressing the ethical and legal implications of WBE. Collaborations between neuroscientists, computer scientists, ethicists, and policymakers will be crucial for advancing this field responsibly.

glossary.def: The theoretical process of creating a digital copy or simulation of a human brain, including its synaptic connections and neural activity patterns.

A type of computing architecture designed to mimic the structure and function of biological neurons and synapses, aiming for more efficient processing of certain types of data like sensory input or complex pattern recognition.
The complete map of neural connections in a brain, including all synaptic links between neurons.

subsystems.name: Specimen preservation
subsystems.role: stabilise the brain so its wiring is fixed at nanometre scale.

subsystems.name: High-resolution imaging
subsystems.role: capture the whole brain at synaptic resolution.

subsystems.name: Image processing
subsystems.role: stitch and align millions of serial images into one 3D volume.

subsystems.name: Connectome reconstruction
subsystems.role: trace every neuron and locate every synapse.

subsystems.name: Neuronal modelling
subsystems.role: turn the wiring diagram into a dynamical model of the brain.

subsystems.name: Simulation platform
subsystems.role: run the model fast enough to behave in real time.

subsystems.name: Data and storage
subsystems.role: hold petabytes of images and simulation state.

buildSteps.title: Preserve the brain
buildSteps.detail: The brain must be fixed and stabilised so that membranes, vesicles and synaptic clefts survive slicing and imaging without distortion.

buildSteps.title: Cut and image
buildSteps.detail: The tissue is sliced into nanometre-thin sections and imaged with electron microscopes, section by section, across the entire volume.

buildSteps.title: Align the images
buildSteps.detail: Millions of images are computationally stitched and aligned into a single continuous 3D dataset.

buildSteps.title: Segment the wiring
buildSteps.detail: Algorithms trace each neuron’s branches and mark chemical synapses where one cell meets another.

buildSteps.title: Map the connectome
buildSteps.detail: The result is a graph of neurons and connections, annotated with cell types and synapse properties.

buildSteps.title: Build a dynamical model
buildSteps.detail: Each neuron type is given equations for its ion channels and each synapse a strength and time course, turning the wiring diagram into a working model.

buildSteps.title: Simulate the network
buildSteps.detail: The model is run on specialised hardware or supercomputers, aiming to match the brain’s electrical activity in real time.

buildSteps.title: Validate against behaviour
buildSteps.detail: The emulation is tested by comparing its outputs with recordings from the original brain or organism.

prerequisites.why: no human brain has been mapped at this scale; even complete maps of small mammals do not yet exist.
many ion channels and synapse types are known, but not all, and their variation across cell types is incompletely understood.
supercomputers now reach exaflop speeds, but simulating a human brain in real time is many orders of magnitude beyond current capacity.
chemical fixation and cryopreservation preserve ultrastructure in small samples, but preserving an entire human brain without damage is unproven.
no test exists to confirm that a simulation has subjective experience or matches the original person’s mind.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small organisms and partial maps of larger brains
pathway.unlocks: methods for imaging, segmentation and circuit modelling.

pathway.milestone: full connectome of a small mammal and simulation of its basic circuits
pathway.unlocks: proof that a complete wiring diagram can be turned into working behaviour.

pathway.milestone: whole-brain emulation of a small mammal with behavioural validation
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the approach scales and that emulations can be compared with the original.

pathway.milestone: human whole-brain emulation, if scanning, computing and validation problems are solved
pathway.unlocks: a possible route to digital immortality, but also profound ethical and legal questions.
